## Current work

The mammalian heart is among the tissues that can regenerate shortly after birth
but lose this capacity within the first week of life. My postdoctoral work
revealed that successful cardiac regeneration depends on active,
developmentally restricted immune programs, rather than on the immature or
attenuated immune state traditionally associated with the neonatal period. I
first demonstrated that the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint pathway is highly
active in the neonatal heart and required for regeneration after myocardial
infarction. Disruption of this pathway altered the neonatal γδ T cell behavior,
promoting cytotoxic and autoreactive features, excessive inflammation, and
fibrotic repair. I subsequently identified these γδ T cells as a population of
γδT17 cells that accumulates in the injured heart specifically during the
regenerative window and supports regeneration through IL-17A. I further showed
that IL-17A acts primarily on macrophages and monocytes to initiate a rapid,
self-limited inflammatory response that supports injury resolution.

## Research funding

**T cell-mediated regulation of mouse neonatal heart regeneration.** American
Heart Association, 2025–2028 ([Award No. 25CDA1454364](https://doi.org/10.58275/AHA.25CDA1454364.pc.gr.229577)).
This project studies how neonatal γδ T cells and IL-17A support heart regeneration
and whether IL-17A can improve repair after the regenerative window closes.

**The role of monocyte infiltration in cardiac regeneration and repair.** American
Heart Association, 2022–2024 (Award No. 916883).
This project examined whether sustained monocyte recruitment shifts the injured
neonatal heart from regeneration toward fibrotic repair.
